cards.vorderseite: Resting membrane potential: what determines it
cards.rueckseite:
About **−90 mV** in large myelinated fibers and skeletal muscle (−65 mV in neuronal soma). Set mainly by **K⁺** (equilibrium potential −94 mV) because resting K⁺ permeability is ~100× that of Na⁺ (E_Na +61 mV). Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves **3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in**.
Nernst: E = ±61 log (C_out/C_in).

cards.vorderseite: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channel: gates and refractory period
cards.rueckseite:
Outer **activation gate** (closed at rest, opens at threshold) and inner **inactivation gate** (closes shortly after). Inactivation persists until repolarization → **absolute refractory period**; relative refractory period follows (supranormal stimulus needed). K⁺ channels open slowly → repolarization and after-hyperpolarization.
**Tetrodotoxin** blocks Na⁺ channels; **TEA** blocks K⁺ channels.

**Stabilize (less excitable):** hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, local anesthetics, acidosis.
**Destabilize (more excitable):** **hypocalcemia** (Na⁺ channels open at more negative potentials → tetany), hyperkalemia, **alkalosis** (why hyperventilation provokes seizures), caffeine, strychnine.

Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance; AP jumps between **nodes of Ranvier** (every 1–3 mm). Faster and energy-efficient. Velocity: unmyelinated ~0.5 m/s, large myelinated up to ~120 m/s. Peripheral nerves contain more unmyelinated than myelinated fibers.

cards.rueckseite:
AP → opening of presynaptic **voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels** → Ca²⁺ influx → vesicle fusion and transmitter release (1 vesicle = 1 **quantum** → miniature endplate potential). Cleft 20–30 nm. Postsynaptic: ionotropic (fast) or G-protein/second messenger (slow) receptors.
Blocked release: **botulinum toxin** (SNARE cleavage), **Lambert–Eaton** (antibodies vs. presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels).

Ligand-gated **Cl⁻ channel** (pentamer). **Benzodiazepines** bind the α/γ interface → increase **frequency** of opening. **Barbiturates** → increase **duration** of opening (and directly open at high dose). Blocked by picrotoxin, bicuculline.
GABA-B: G-protein, ↑ K⁺ conductance; agonist **baclofen**.

Glutamate receptor that is both **ligand-gated** (glutamate + **glycine co-agonist**) and **voltage-dependent** (Mg²⁺ block removed by depolarization). Permeable to **Ca²⁺**, Na⁺, K⁺ → synaptic plasticity (LTP) and **excitotoxicity**. Antagonists: ketamine, memantine.

cards.rueckseite: Melzack and Wall (1965): activity in large myelinated **Aβ** fibers inhibits transmission of nociceptive Aδ/C input in the **substantia gelatinosa** (lamina II). Basis for TENS and **spinal cord stimulation**. Endogenous opioids (enkephalins) inhibit C and Aδ terminals presynaptically in laminae I, II, V.

After a lesion (usually stroke) of the **VPL/VPM thalamus**: initial contralateral hemianesthesia, followed by severe, burning **contralateral pain** and allodynia/hyperpathia. Central (deafferentation) pain; treatment difficult (antiepileptics, antidepressants, motor cortex or deep brain stimulation).

cards.vorderseite: Muscle spindle vs. Golgi tendon organ
cards.rueckseite:
**Muscle spindle** (parallel to extrafibers, Ia/II afferents, γ efferents): senses **length/stretch** → stretch reflex (monosynaptic, contraction).
**Golgi tendon organ** (in series, Ib): senses **tension** → inhibits the agonist (autogenic inhibition, "clasp-knife" phenomenon).
**Renshaw cells:** recurrent inhibition of α motor neurons (glycine).

**Decorticate** (flexion of arms, extension of legs): lesion **above the red nucleus** (hemisphere, internal capsule, thalamus); rubrospinal tract facilitates arm flexors.
**Decerebrate** (extension of all limbs): lesion **between red nucleus and vestibular nuclei** (midbrain/upper pons); unopposed lateral vestibulospinal/pontine reticulospinal extensor drive. Worse prognosis.

**Semicircular canals** (ampulla, cupula): **angular acceleration** (rotation).
**Utricle** (horizontal) and **saccule** (vertical) maculae with otoconia: **linear acceleration** and head tilt/gravity.
Caloric testing (COWS): **C**old water → nystagmus fast phase to the **O**pposite side, **W**arm → **S**ame side. In coma with intact brainstem: cold water → tonic deviation **toward** the irrigated ear.

zeilen: Loss of striatal GABA/ACh neurons (caudate atrophy)

cards.rueckseite: Violent, flinging movements of the **contralateral** limbs from a lesion of the **subthalamic nucleus** (classically lacunar stroke): loss of STN excitation of GPi → disinhibition of thalamus. Often improves spontaneously.

Consolidation of new declarative memory needs the **hippocampus** (and DM thalamus, mammillary bodies). Bilateral hippocampal resection (patient H.M.) → **anterograde amnesia**, remote memories and procedural learning preserved. Retrograde amnesia affects **recent** memories more than old ones. Procedural memory: basal ganglia, cerebellum.

zeilen: Deep (slow-wave) sleep, infants; awake adult = pathology

cards.rueckseite:
**Non-REM (slow-wave) ~75%:** N1 (θ), N2 (**sleep spindles, K complexes**), N3 (δ waves; deep sleep; sleepwalking, night terrors).
**REM ~25%:** every ~90 min, desynchronized EEG, rapid eye movements, **muscle atonia**, dreams, ↑ variability of HR/BP. REM generated in the **pons** (cholinergic); locus coeruleus/raphe modulate.

cards.vorderseite: Autonomic nervous system: transmitters and receptors
cards.rueckseite:
All **preganglionic** fibers: ACh → **nicotinic** receptors.
Postganglionic **parasympathetic**: ACh → muscarinic.
Postganglionic **sympathetic**: NE → α/β; exceptions: **sweat glands** (ACh, muscarinic), adrenal medulla (preganglionic, releases epinephrine).
Sympathetic outflow T1–L2 (thoracolumbar); parasympathetic CN III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4 (craniosacral).

**Parasympathetic (S2–S4, pelvic nerve):** detrusor contraction → voiding.
**Sympathetic (T10–L2, hypogastric nerve):** detrusor relaxation, internal sphincter contraction → storage.
**Somatic (S2–S4, pudendal nerve):** external sphincter.
**Pontine micturition center** coordinates; lesions above the pons → uninhibited bladder, between pons and sacrum → detrusor–sphincter dyssynergia, sacral/cauda → atonic overflow bladder.

Normal CBF ~**50 mL/100 g/min**. **Autoregulation** keeps CBF constant over MAP ~50–150 mmHg (shifted right in chronic hypertension; lost in injured brain).
**PaCO₂:** CBF changes ~**2–4% per mmHg** (linear between 20–80 mmHg) → hyperventilation lowers ICP but risks ischemia.
**PaO₂:** CBF rises only when PaO₂ < 50 mmHg.
Flow–metabolism coupling: ↑ activity → ↑ CBF.

**Myasthenia gravis:** antibodies vs. postsynaptic **ACh receptor** (or MuSK) → fatigable weakness, **decrement** on repetitive stimulation.
**Lambert–Eaton:** antibodies vs. presynaptic **P/Q Ca²⁺ channels** (small cell lung cancer) → weakness that **improves with exercise**, **increment** at high-frequency stimulation, areflexia, autonomic symptoms.
**Botulism:** blocks ACh release (SNAP-25).

**Succinylcholine (depolarizing):** persistent depolarization; no fade; potentiated by cholinesterase inhibitors; risks: **hyperkalemia** (denervation, burns, SCI, immobilization), malignant hyperthermia, ↑ ICP/IOP.
**Nondepolarizing** (rocuronium, vecuronium): competitive; train-of-four **fade**; reversed by neostigmine (+ glycopyrrolate) or **sugammadex** (rocuronium/vecuronium).

Motor unit = one α motor neuron + all muscle fibers it innervates (few fibers for eye muscles, thousands for leg muscles). **Henneman size principle:** small (slow, fatigue-resistant, type I) units are recruited first, large (fast, type II) units later. Reinnervation after denervation → large polyphasic motor unit potentials on EMG.
